questions.evidence:
In a classroom scenario, a team compares two cloth squares under a sunny window. One is black cotton and the other is white cotton. The squares have the same size and thickness. The teacher places a temperature sensor beneath each and starts the observation together.

After fifteen minutes, the reading under the black square is thirty-five degrees Celsius, while the white square reads thirty-one. Both began at twenty-eight degrees. The group records the starting and ending values instead of reporting only the higher final number.

They repeat the comparison after switching the squares' left and right positions. This helps them check whether one part of the windowsill receives different sunlight. They keep the same observation time and use the same two sensors throughout the activity.

The first round suggests a difference under these conditions, but the team avoids a claim about all black and white objects everywhere. Other materials, locations, or weather could change the results. The report includes the setup so readers can understand what the numbers actually compare.
questions.explanation: 只就此材料、環境與程序下的結果陳述。
options: These squares showed different changes in the stated setup.
Position can never affect a window experiment.
Every black object is always four degrees warmer.
questions.prompt: Which conclusion stays within the evidence?

lessons.story:
In a classroom scenario, a team compares two cloth squares under a sunny window. One is black cotton and the other is white cotton. The squares have the same size and thickness. The teacher places a temperature sensor beneath each and starts the observation together.

After fifteen minutes, the reading under the black square is thirty-five degrees Celsius, while the white square reads thirty-one. Both began at twenty-eight degrees. The group records the starting and ending values instead of reporting only the higher final number.

They repeat the comparison after switching the squares' left and right positions. This helps them check whether one part of the windowsill receives different sunlight. They keep the same observation time and use the same two sensors throughout the activity.

The first round suggests a difference under these conditions, but the team avoids a claim about all black and white objects everywhere. Other materials, locations, or weather could change the results. The report includes the setup so readers can understand what the numbers actually compare.
